# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | In Progress          |

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults.
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake.

## Schema compilation and caching

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at registration time naming the tool for an uncompilable schema](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).
- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema`.
- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules.

## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery

- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults.
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake.

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at registration time naming the tool for an uncompilable schema](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).

# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | Shipped              |

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16), [validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L24)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46), [validated by: rejects a wrong-typed field naming the path and expected type, without the offending value](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L50)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults ([validated by: passes valid input through to the executor unchanged, extra properties included, exactly once](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L80)).
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake ([validated by: throws Unknown tool for an unregistered name](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L108)).

## Schema compilation and caching

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at registration time naming the tool for an uncompilable schema](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).
- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema` ([validated by: reuses the schema compiled at register time across ten execute calls](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L149)).
- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules ([validated by: validates a function-valued source against the schema current at each call](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L114)).

## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery

- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).

# Changelog

All notable changes to `@re-cinq/hal-engine` are documented here.

The format is [Keep a Changelog 1.1.0](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project adheres to
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html). Entries are written for somebody installing the
package, not for somebody reading this repository's commit log.

## [Unreleased]

### Changed

- **Breaking:** `ToolRegistry.register` now compiles a tool's `inputSchema` with `ajv` (`strict: false`, `validateFormats: false`) at registration time and throws naming the tool when the schema is not valid JSON Schema.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-09-17

### Changed

- `HalEngineConfig.orchestrator.hooks` now carries a JSDoc comment. The field already shipped
  in `0.2.x`; the comment makes the lifecycle-hook seam discoverable from the published type
  declarations so editors surface it on hover without a trip to the README.

## [0.2.1] - 2026-09-14

Identical to `0.2.0` — same files, same code. It exists to prove that a release publishes with no
credential stored in the repository: `0.2.0` had to be published with a token, because the registry
cannot hold a trusted publisher for a name that has never been published, and this is the first version
released through that publisher instead. There is nothing here to upgrade for.

## [0.2.0] - 2026-09-14

The first release under the `@re-cinq` scope. Nothing has been published before it, so there is no upgrade
path from `0.1.0` on the registry — only from the git specifier.

### Changed

- The published package carries no source maps. `files` is `["dist"]`, so every `.js.map` and `.d.ts.map`
  named a `../src/*.ts` the tarball did not contain and carried no inlined sources — 98 files that resolved
  to nothing in a debugger. Dropping them halves the file count. Step through the source from a checkout
  of the repository instead.

- The README documents the three environment variables this package actually reads — `CORS_ORIGIN`, `PORT`
  and `LOG_LEVEL` — each with its reading site, what overrides it, and its default. `AWS_REGION` and
  `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` are gone from the provider docs: both are config fields, and setting the variable
  while passing a different `region` or `projectId` silently gives you the config value. Vendor credential
  variables are still listed, now stating that this package reads none of them — the vendor SDK does.

- The README now states which install path is supported. The registry specifier is the product; a git
  specifier builds from a checkout, carries no provenance, and pins a commit rather than a version. If you
  install from git under the key `hal-engine`, note that the rename is silent — `import 'hal-engine'` keeps
  working and `import '@re-cinq/hal-engine'` is what fails, because npm installs under the dependency key
  rather than the package name.

- **Log output is JSON, one object per line.** Lines were unstructured text (`[time] [LEVEL] [category] msg`),
  so `log.error` was indistinguishable from `log.info` to anything reading the stream. Each line now carries
  `severity`, `message`, `timestamp` and `category`, with the call site's fields under `data`. `ERROR` goes to
  stderr; every other level goes to stdout. If you parse this output, it has changed shape — see
  [docs/logging.md](docs/logging.md). Supply your own `logger` in `HalEngineConfig` to keep the old format, or
  any other — the option now reaches the package's own log calls, which it did not before this release. The
  swap is process-wide rather than per engine; `docs/logging.md` says why.

- The demo chat routes log a refusal. Every `401` emits one `warn` on category `http` carrying a fixed
  reason and nothing derived from the request, so a denied call is auditable without the log becoming a
  second place the request leaks.

- `engine.start()` rejects when the port is unavailable, instead of ending the process. There was no `error`
  listener on the HTTP server, so an `EADDRINUSE` surfaced as an unhandled event while the promise `start()`
  returned never settled — uncatchable, unretryable. The "HAL Engine started" line now logs the port that was
  actually bound rather than the one requested, which is what `transport.port: 0` makes visible.

- An optional provider SDK that is installed but has a missing dependency of its own now surfaces the loader's
  real error. It was reported as the peer being absent, so the message told you to install a package you
  already had and discarded the actual cause.

- A log call can no longer throw, whichever logger is installed. `data` that cannot be serialised — a circular
  reference, a `BigInt` — is written as `"[unserialisable]: <reason>"` with the rest of the line intact,
  instead of raising a `TypeError` out of whatever was being logged. A `WsAuthenticator` returning an identity
  with a back-reference used to take down the connection that carried it and leave its session in the store.
  A supplied `logger` that throws is caught the same way, and its line goes to the console so that it is not
  lost — which means a logger that writes and then throws emits it twice. See
  [docs/logging.md](docs/logging.md).

- `LOG_LEVEL` gates a supplied `logger` exactly as it gates the built-in one. The threshold is tested once
  before dispatch, so a level below it never reaches your implementation.

- `setLogger` is exported, so a logger installed through `HalEngineConfig` can be replaced or put back.
  Calling it with no argument restores the built-in console logger. Note that the swap is process-wide:
  `createHalEngine` installs a logger only when the config names one, so a second engine that names none keeps
  using whatever was last set. [docs/logging.md](docs/logging.md) says why.

- **Breaking: the package is ESM-only.** `require('@re-cinq/hal-engine')` no longer works. Use
  `import` from an ESM module, or stay on the git specifier until you can. The package declares
  `"type": "module"` and resolves through an `exports` map.
- **Breaking: renamed from `hal-engine` to `@re-cinq/hal-engine`.** Update the specifier in every
  `import` and in `package.json`. A dependency installed from a git specifier resolves under its
  entry **key**, not the package's `name`, so an existing `"hal-engine": "github:…"` entry keeps
  working silently — it will not tell you the package has been renamed.
- An absent optional provider SDK now fails when you construct that provider, not when you import the
  package, and raises an `AIError` with code `OPTIONAL_PEER_MISSING` naming the package and the command
  that installs it, instead of a raw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` from inside `dist/`.
- Node 22 or newer is required, declared in `engines`.

### Added

- `LICENSE` (Apache-2.0), declared in `package.json`.
- `exports`, `repository`, `engines` and `publishConfig` entries in the manifest.
- `AuthenticatedRequest` is exported from the package root: `Request` plus an optional `user`, for typing
  the `auth.http` middleware you supply. `HttpAuthMiddleware` is stated in its terms rather than as a bare
  Express `RequestHandler`.
- Provenance. This is the first version on the registry, and it and every version after it carry an npm
  provenance attestation: `npm audit signatures` verifies that the tarball was built by a workflow in this
  repository's CI from the commit the attestation names, rather than uploaded by whoever held a token. This
  version is the one exception to how the rest are made: a name that has never been published cannot hold
  a trusted publisher, so `0.2.0` was published by a single-use workflow started by hand, and every version
  after it is published by the release workflow from a published GitHub release, with no token anywhere. It is attestable
  because the source repository is public, which [ADR-007](adrs/ADR-007-repository-visibility.md) decided
  and gives the reasoning for.

### Removed

- **Breaking: the `send_message` frame type is gone.** The WebSocket server accepted it as an alias for
  `user_message` and normalised it away. Send `user_message` instead; an alias frame now comes back as an
  `error` with code `INVALID_MESSAGE`. The exported `IncomingMessage` union never contained the alias, so
  TypeScript clients were already writing `user_message` — this affects hand-written JSON frames, including
  the one the old quick start showed.

### Fixed

- `setLogger(log)` and `logger: log` in `HalEngineConfig` no longer silence the engine. Handing the package's
  own `log` object back to it made every call recurse until the stack ran out, and the overflow was swallowed,
  so nothing was written and nothing failed. It is now treated as passing no logger: the console one is used.
  The full configuration example did exactly this; it now shows a logger of its own.
- `stop()` resolves after a `start()` that was refused, and after a second `stop()`, instead of rejecting with
  `ERR_SERVER_NOT_RUNNING`. A bind failure inside `try { await start() } finally { await stop() }` used to
  surface twice.
- Calling `start()` on a running server is refused with `HAL Engine is already started` and leaves the server
  as it was. It used to reject too, but only after removing the persistent `error` handler, so the next socket
  error on the still-running server ended the process.
- `orchestrator.hooks` is reachable through `createHalEngine`. `OrchestratorHooks` was documented but the
  factory forwarded only `maxToolRounds` and `contextConfig`, so every hook was silently dropped. Assembling
  the parts by hand is no longer the only way to use them.
- `transport.port` is honoured. It was declared on the config and never forwarded, so the server always fell
  through to `PORT` or `8086`. Resolution order is now the `start(port)` argument, then `transport.port`,
  then `PORT`, then `8086` — and `transport.port: 0` means "let the OS choose", not `8086`.
- An engine that is constructed but never started no longer keeps the process alive. The WebSocket heartbeat
  timer is `unref`ed, so the listening socket is what holds Node open, as it should be.

- Every documented model id is one the vendor still serves. Six of the seven in the docs and fixtures were
  dead or dying as of 2026-09-11 — two Claude 3 models past or at end-of-life on Bedrock, Claude Sonnet 4
  legacy on Bedrock and retired on Anthropic's own API, and both Gemini 1.5 ids gone from Vertex. `modelId`
  is an unvalidated string, so a retired id reaches you as an error that looks like your credentials are
  wrong. Bedrock examples now carry the `eu.` geo inference profile prefix, which Claude Sonnet 4.5 requires
  because it supports no in-region inference.

- The README provider table scores each provider per method. `AIProvider` has two methods and Bedrock
  implements only one — its `generateStructured` throws while Vertex's works — so two rows previously read
  `Full` while one provider did half of what the other did. Each cell now names `Implemented` or the message
  it throws, and the "switching providers is config-only" claim is qualified: it holds for `sendMessage` and
  not for `generateStructured`, with no compile-time signal either way.

- The README quick start and `docs/getting-started.md` now match the API. Both showed `PromptBuilderConfig`
  fields that do not exist (`guidelines`, `context`, `customInstructions` for `responseGuidelines`,
  `domainContext`, `toolPreamble`), a `ws` authenticator taking a token rather than the upgrade request and
  returning `userId` rather than `id`, and an `engine.listen()` that was never an API. `example/server.ts` is
  type-checked in CI now, and both documents are written against it.
- `docs/getting-started.md` no longer documents `orchestrator.hooks` on `HalEngineConfig`. `createHalEngine`
  forwards only `maxToolRounds` and `contextConfig`, so the hooks were unreachable that way; the guide now
  shows `createChatOrchestrator`, which is where they work.

- `onConnect` is now called. It was declared on the config, forwarded through `createHalEngine`, and then
  dropped before the connection handler ever saw it, so it never fired — while its sibling `onDisconnect`
  worked, which is what made the gap hard to notice. It runs once per accepted connection, after the
  `connected` frame.
- Neither lifecycle hook can take a connection down. Both now return `void | Promise<void>`, are never
  awaited, and route through one helper that logs and swallows a throw or a rejection. A rejecting
  `onDisconnect` previously reached the process as an unhandled rejection, which ends it under Node's
  defaults.

- Importing the package root no longer loads the Google Vertex AI SDK. It previously pulled in 38
  `@google-cloud/vertexai` modules whether or not you used Vertex, so a consumer of the mock or Bedrock
  provider could not install without it.
- Consumers can type-check against the published declarations. `@types/express`, `@types/node` and
  `@types/ws` are runtime dependencies now; the emitted `.d.ts` files import `express`, `http`, `stream`
  and `ws`, so with those packages dev-only a consumer resolved the runtime and then failed to compile.
- An Express `RequestHandler` can be assigned to `HttpAuthMiddleware`. The option was declared returning
  `void | Promise<void>` while Express declares its handlers `unknown`, so every middleware a consumer
  already had was refused by `tsc` and had to be re-typed or cast. The return is `unknown` now; nothing
  reads it.

- `createProvider({type: 'mock', structuredResponses})` now honours `structuredResponses`. It previously
  dropped the configuration, so the same config object behaved differently through `createProvider` than
  through `createMockProvider`. Note that the map configures `generateStructured`, which nothing inside
  `createHalEngine` calls.
- Compiled test files are no longer published in `dist/`.

### Security

- **There is somewhere to report a vulnerability.** `SECURITY.md` states the intake address, a 48-hour
  acknowledgement target, supported versions, coordinated disclosure, and what is in and out of scope. The
  address is in `package.json`'s `bugs`, so `npm view @re-cinq/hal-engine bugs` finds it without repository
  access.
- **Breaking: the HTTP chat routes deny by default.** With no `auth.http` middleware configured,
  `POST /chats`, `GET /chats/:id` and `POST /chats/:id/messages` now answer `401 Unauthorized`. They
  previously served every caller as one shared `anonymous` user, so anyone holding a chat id could read
  and post to it. Configure `auth.http` to keep them reachable.
- **Breaking: the chat routes require an identified user.** Middleware that runs but attaches no `user`,
